en: The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai says:
Second, regarding the opening and closing of the various objects (*viṣaya*), one first takes the "Ten Suchnesses" (*daśa-tathatā*) as the primary focus. Why?
Because this sutra, in its introductory chapter, transcends words to extol these Ten Suchnesses. Now, we further discuss the five objects; how do they correspond or differ?

Is it so? Regarding the opening and closing of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*): they are said to "open" because their names differ, and they are said to "close" because their meaning is the same.
The link of ignorance (*avidyā*) corresponds to the suchness of suchness-nature (*tathatā-tathatā*).
The link of volitional formations (saṃskāra) is associated with such characteristics;
consciousness (vijñāna), name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), contact (sparśa), and feeling (vedanā) are associated with such entities;
craving (tṛṣṇā) is associated with such conditions.
It is grasped in accordance with such power and action;
there is a conjunction with such causes.
Birth, old age, and death are conjoined with such fruits, retributions, and so forth, and so on.
Furthermore, regarding the synthesis: there are two branches that are combined in this manner through their characteristics;
three branches—ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—are combined in this manner through their nature;
and seven branches—from consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—are combined in this manner through their substance.
Thus, this power is still the three links of the path of afflictions (*kleśa*): ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are able to produce the power of karma.
Such activity is still the two links of formative action (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), which are able to perform the work of producing suffering.
In this way, the causes consist of the two links of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), which act as the cause for the seven types of suffering.
In this way, the conditions consist of the three links of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*), which are able to moisten karma and bring about suffering.
In this way, the fruit is itself the habitual result (*vāsanā-phala*) of formative action (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*).
In this way, the retribution (*vipāka*) is itself the karma of formative action and becoming, which summons the retribution of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth.
These two sets both employ the twelve links of dependent origination as they are conventionally conceived, which correspond to the six realms and the ten suchnesses.

Next, employing the inconceivable twelve links of dependent origination to correspond to the four noble ones and their ten suchnesses: when the link of ignorance transforms, it becomes clarity; this clarity is the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*), which constitutes the nature of suchness of the noble ones.
When the factors of unwholesome conduct are transformed, they become wholesome conduct; this wholesome conduct serves as the causal condition for attaining such characteristics of a sage.
When the path of suffering—consisting of consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth—is transformed, it becomes the Dharma-body, thereby constituting the essence of a sage.
The two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) transform into the bodhicitta of a noble one; such is their power.

The link of existence (*bhava*), which contains the fruit, transforms into the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*); thus it becomes the activity of a noble one and also transforms into the cause of a noble one.
This turning of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is of two kinds:
the turning of the Right Path constitutes such causes, while the turning of the Aids to the Path constitutes such conditions for the Noble One (*ārya*).

The turning of the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇāṅga*) constitutes the eternal abiding of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and constitutes such fruits and retributions for the Noble One, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the "total agent," the three factors of essence, power, and activity are themselves afflictions, karma, and suffering, which transform into the Dharma-body, bodhicitta, and the practice of the six perfections.

Diligently practicing these three dharmas: within, they form one's nature; without, they form one's characteristics; with right intention, they form the substance; with far-reaching vows, they form power; by establishing practice, they form activity; by drawing forth results, they form causes; by assisting one another, they form conditions; and by manifesting them, they form fruits and retributions, and so forth.
If one were to subdivide the four types of noble ones, there would be differences in each category; however, as we are now taking the general outline, this is explained in a comprehensive manner.
The Sūtra says:
"The vow for all-knowledge still remains and has not been lost."
The Two Vehicles may also provide a general explanation.

Regarding the fourfold Four Noble Truths combined with the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*): the two types of suffering and origin—namely, those of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising—constitute the ten suchnesses of the six realms of existence.
Such characteristics, such nature, constitute origination (*samudaya*).
Such essence constitutes suffering (*duḥkha*).
Such activity, power, cause, and condition likewise constitute origination.
Thus, such fruits and retributions are also suffering, and so forth.
The two paths of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising, as well as their cessation, constitute the ten suchnesses of the analytical and intrinsic vehicles, as well as the Shared Bodhisattva vehicle.
Such characteristics and nature are themselves the Path.
Such essence is itself cessation.
Such powers, activities, causes, and conditions are all the Path.
Thus, these fruits and retributions are also subject to cessation.
The two kinds of suffering and its accumulation—immeasurable and unconditioned—are precisely the ten suchnesses of the fruit and retribution outside the four noble realms.
The Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) refers to such characteristics, natures, powers, activities, causes, and conditions outside the realm.
The Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) refers to such entities, fruits, retributions, and so forth outside the realm.
The two paths of the immeasurable and the unconditioned, when extinguished, are precisely the ten suchnesses of nirvana beyond the four noble realms.
The Truth of the Path is itself the nature, characteristics, powers, functions, causes, conditions, and so forth of nirvana; it is also prajñā and liberation.
The Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is precisely the essence, fruit, and retribution of *nirvāṇa*, and it also constitutes the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*, and so forth.

Regarding the synthesis of the fourfold Four Noble Truths with the fourfold Twelve Links of Dependent Origination: the two types of suffering and its origin—the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising—correspond respectively to the two types of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination that are subject to deliberation (*cintya*).

The two paths of cessation—arising-and-ceasing and non-arising—are precisely the two types of contemplative analysis regarding the twelve links of dependent origination: from the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death.
The two accumulations of suffering—the immeasurable and the unconditioned—are precisely the two inconceivable twelvefold chains of dependent origination.

The two cessations of the path—the immeasurable and the unconditioned—are likewise the two inconceivable twelvefold chains of dependent origination, from the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death; this is intelligible.

Regarding the seven kinds of two truths combined with the ten suchnesses: the Zang, Tong, Bie, and Yuan [teachings], when categorized by their entry into the common [realm], all share the same four conventional truths, which are the ten suchnesses of the six paths of existence.
The two truths of the *Zang* (Treasure) and *Tong* (Common) vehicles constitute the ten suchnesses of the Two Vehicles.
The *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) [truths] enter into the two conventionalities of the *Bie*:
the conventionality of having limits refers to the ten suchnesses of the six realms of existence.
The "boundless" refers to the ten suchnesses of the Two Vehicles.
The "perfect conventional" (yuan-su) encompasses the ten suchnesses of all nine dharma-realms.

There are five kinds of "true" (zhen): entering the Shared from the Distinct, entering the Shared from the Perfect, entering the Distinct from the Perfect, and entering the Distinct and the Perfect from the Distinct; these are all the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-dharma realm.

Regarding the combination of the seven kinds of two truths with the four kinds of twelvefold dependent origination: the Zang, Tong, Bie, and Yuan [teachings] each have their own entry into the conventional truth for ordinary beings, totaling four types of conventional truth; these constitute the two kinds of twelvefold dependent origination that are subject to conceptual thought.

The two truths of the Tripitaka and Shared [vehicles] are the twelve links of dependent origination as subject to conceptual thought, from the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death.
The Separate and Complete [vehicles] enter into the two conventionalities of the Separate:
the side of existence is the twelve links of dependent origination as subject to conceptual thought;
The boundless is the cessation of conceptual ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death;
this encompasses both the conventional and the ultimate, penetrating the four types of twelvefold dependent origination within and beyond the triple world.

There are five kinds of truth: entering the Separate through the Universal, entering the Universal through the Separate, entering the Separate through the Universal, and the Separate and Universal [together]. These are the inconceivable twelve links of dependent origination outside the triple world, ranging from the extinction of ignorance up to the extinction of old age and death.
Regarding the synthesis of the seven kinds of two truths with the four kinds of four truths: the ultimate has two truths, which are the four truths of arising and ceasing;
the illusory has two truths, which are the four truths of non-arising.
The Separate and Common [Vehicles] entering the conventional truth both pertain to the suffering and its origin as non-arising;
the Separate and Common [Vehicles] entering the ultimate truth pertain to the path and cessation as immeasurable.
Rounding into and penetrating the ultimate truth is the unconditioned path and cessation.
Distinguishing the conventional and rounding into and penetrating the conventional—this is the immeasurable suffering and origin.
Rounding the conventional is the unconditioned suffering and origin.
The distinct truth is the cessation of the immeasurable path.
Entering the distinct truth and the perfect truth is the cessation of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) path.

As for the five kinds of three truths combined into ten suchnesses (*tathatā*): the distinct entry into the common and the perfect entry into the common both involve the two conventional truths; these are the ten suchnesses of the six paths.
Distinct conventionality refers to the ten suchnesses of the six realms when one enters distinct conventionality;
"with limit" refers to the ten suchnesses of the two vehicles.
As for perfect conventionality, its meaning extends throughout the nine realms, and so forth.
The five kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) are all the ten suchnesses (*yathābhūta*) of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas;
the five kinds of middle truth (*madhyama-satya*) are all the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm.

As for the five kinds of three truths combined with the four kinds of twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), these consist of the two conventional truths (*saṃvṛti*) of both the Separate (*vyavasthāna*) and the Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) [teachings], which are the twelvefold dependent origination that is conceivable by the six classes of beings.
The Separate and Perfect [Vehicles] enter into two types of conventional truth:
"having limits" refers to the conceptualization of the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination within the six realms;
"being limitless" refers to the conceptualization of the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
The distinction between the ultimate and the conventional is explained extensively in various contexts.

For now, we shall employ these four types of twelvefold dependent origination; the fivefold truth is precisely the cessation of the conceivable twelvefold dependent origination, which is also the arising of the inconceivable twelvefold dependent origination.
Among the five kinds [of truths], the ultimate truth is precisely the cessation of the inconceivable twelvefold dependent origination.

As for the combination of the three truths of the five kinds with the four truths of the four kinds: the distinct [teaching] enters into the common, and the perfect [teaching] enters into both the common and the particular; this is the non-arising of suffering and its origin.

The distinct conventional, the perfect entry into the distinct conventional, and the perfect conventional are all, in common, the unarisen accumulation of suffering; they are also the unarisen path and cessation, and they are also the immeasurable accumulation of suffering.
The Separate [Vehicle] enters through the Common and Round [Vehicles] into both truths; its original focus is on the side of mere emptiness, which is the Path and Cessation of non-arising.
The Separate Truth and the Round entry into the Separate Truth are themselves the Path and Cessation of non-arising; within the immeasurable, these constitute Suffering and Origination.
Yuanzhen, non-arising is the cessation of the path (*mārga-nirodha*); the immeasurable and the unconditioned are the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
Entering the particular within the universal, this is the immeasurable cessation of the path.
Entering the Perfect [Teaching] within the Shared [Teaching], this is the cessation through the path of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-mārga-nirodha*).
Within the Distinct [Teaching], this is the cessation through the immeasurable path (*apramāṇa-mārga-nirodha*).
Entering the Perfect [Teaching] within the Distinct [Teaching], this is the cessation through the path of non-action.
Within the Perfect [Teaching], this precisely refers to the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) Path and Cessation.
Regarding the combination of the five kinds of the Three Truths with the seven kinds of the Two Truths, this excludes the previous two types of the Two Truths from being so combined.
Next, regarding the two kinds of two truths: the two conventionalities are precisely the five kinds of conventionalities within the system of the five kinds of three truths.
The two ultimates consist of the aspect of emptiness, which is the ultimate within the five kinds of three truths;
and the aspect of non-emptiness, which is the middle [truth] within the five kinds of three truths.
Regarding the latter three types of two truths: the three conventional truths and the limit of emptiness constitute the "truth" (paramārtha-satya) of the fivefold three-truth system;
the limit of existence constitutes the "conventional truth" (saṃvṛti-satya) of the fivefold three-truth system.
The "three truths" refer to the five types of the threefold truth (triratna-satya).

Furthermore, there is another way of explaining them: as will be clarified later, the first two truths are not combined; within the latter five conventional truths, there are both the true and the conventional;
within the latter five true truths, there are both the true and the middle.

Regarding the "unification of the single ultimate truth with the ten suchnesses": each and every dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) possesses all ten realms; by eliminating the other nine realms, it remains identical only to the Buddha-dharma realm.
Excluding the three types of twelvefold dependent origination, it is identical only to the single type of twelvefold dependent origination of cessation.
Excluding the three types of four noble truths, it is identical only to the single reality of the four noble truths.
Excluding the sevenfold Two Truths, they merely share similarities and differences with the Five True Truths.
Excluding the fivefold Three Truths, they merely share similarities with the Five Middle Truths, and so forth.
To say that there is no truth and it is ineffable means that it accords with the ten suchnesses; "suchness" (tathatā) signifies non-differentiation, which is itself emptiness and quiescence.
That words and signs are extinguished and cannot be demonstrated is precisely the meaning of all ten being suchness.
The cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death is profoundly deep; this profound depth is identical to the absence of truth.
The arising of birth cannot be spoken of, and even the non-arising of non-birth cannot be spoken of; this is identical to the absence of truth.
The seven kinds of true truths are all inexpressible.
Regarding the fact that the primary true truth is inexpressible, as Śāriputra said:
"I have heard that within liberation there is no verbal expression."
How much more so for the latter six?
It is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa; since it is neither of the two extremes, there is likewise no middle way. Thus, the fivefold Middle Truth is identical to the absence of truth.
One reality is named "space," yet space has no "one"; how, then, can there be reality? This is identical to the truth of non-existence (*an-utpāda*).
Since non-existence itself has nothing in which to abide, the great wisdom of equality is without differentiation.
Although there is no plurality, plurality is immeasurable; when extended, it fills the Dharma-realm, yet one does not know from where it comes.
Immeasurability has no plurality; when withdrawn, nothing remains to be known, yet one does not know where it goes.
"Neither coming nor going" refers to the Dharma-Buddha, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the seven kinds of two truths, they are opened or closed according to conditions, and they turn and enter into one another; each of these, moreover, possesses its own aspects of conforming to worldly sentiment, conforming to both sentiment and wisdom, and conforming to wisdom alone.
The remaining five meanings should likewise be understood by analogy, though they are not recorded here in full. Why?
Because when the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind.
Reflect upon this yourself!
Question:
Since the principles of all objects have already been harmonized, for what reason do they proliferate and further constrain one another?
Answer: The Tathāgata observes and knows the nature and characteristics of the ten realms, seeing those who are matured and those who are not yet matured.
He does not cause those with great capacities whose faculties are not yet matured to give rise to slander.
If the capacities of those of lesser faculties have matured, one must not allow the opportune moment to pass.

According to what is appropriate for each, whether by means of the single or the compound, the partial or the perfect, they should be brought to maturity so that they may derive benefit upon hearing [the teaching].
Although the *Avataṃsaka* fully discerns the ten realms, because two realms are matured, it brings them to maturity through both the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Perfect (Bodhisattva) vehicles.
The Tripitaka also discerns the ten realms, but because the nature and characteristics of the Two Vehicles are matured, it brings them to maturity by means of the doctrine of arising and ceasing.
The Vaipulya [sūtras] also reflect the ten realms; because four realms are matured, they bring them to maturity by means of four kinds of mutual inclusion.
The Prajñā [pāramitā sūtras] also reflect the ten realms; likewise, because four realms are matured, they bring them to maturity by means of three kinds of mutual inclusion.
The Lotus Sūtra likewise reflects upon the ten realms; while their single nature and characteristics are already matured, it brings them to full maturity through the single, perfect truth.
If there were no skillful means to appear and disappear in order to harmonize and mature them, how could object and wisdom attain such fusion and subtlety?

For example, even a painter can blend the five colors with water to create various images; how much more so, then, could the Buddha, the King of Dharma, who possesses mastery over all phenomena, not interweave various means to tame and transform sentient beings?
Question:
Regarding the six objects and so forth explained above, does this sutra allow for the existence of their referents even if they lack names? Answer:
The names and meanings of the ten suchnesses have already been fully set forth above.
Regarding the four kinds of twelvefold dependent origination: the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter elucidates the twelvefold dependent origination of arising and ceasing;
the "Parable" chapter clarifies the twelvefold dependent origination of non-arising, which consists simply in being free from delusion.
The "Expedient Means" chapter states:

"The Buddha-seed arises from conditions. This refers to the two types of twelvefold dependent origination—immeasurable and unconditioned—which exist beyond the realm of conditioned phenomena (*dhātu*).
Regarding the fourfold Four Noble Truths: the "Parable" chapter explains that the cause of all suffering is rooted in craving; these are the Four Truths of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
In the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter, the thorough realization of the dharma of emptiness refers to the four truths of non-arising.

Furthermore, it speaks of the "unsurpassed path," and in the "Expedient Means" chapter, it mentions only the "unsurpassed path" and the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa; these refer to the two types of four truths—the immeasurable and the unconditioned—which belong to the realm beyond [the threefold world].
The ten such distinctions belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Only Buddhas, together with Buddhas, are able to exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
As stated in the "Peaceful Conduct" (*Anrakugyō*) chapter:
"Furthermore, one does not discriminate between conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, nor between real and unreal phenomena.
Existence is conventional truth;
non-existence is ultimate truth.
"Furthermore, not making conceptual distinctions" serves to negate the two extremes and reveal the Middle Way.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Chapter on Lifespan) states:
"Neither identical nor different. "Not different" does not refer to the conventional, and "not identical" does not refer to the ultimate; this is the meaning of the Three Truths.
The "Expedient Means" chapter states:
"Furthermore, by means of other expedient devices, one assists in manifesting the primary meaning.
This refers to the single ultimate truth.
It is further said:
"This alone is the one true reality.

If one says, "I preach the Dharma of non-discrimination," and again, "The mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words," this is the meaning of the absence of [conventional] truth.
Second, regarding the "Excellence of Wisdom": the ultimate principle is profound and subtle; without wisdom, it cannot be revealed.
Wisdom is able to know its object, yet it would not be integrated were it not for that object.

Since the object is both integrated and sublime, wisdom is commensurate with it—just like a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound. Therefore, wisdom is explained immediately after the object.
Wisdom is divided into two parts:
first, a general discussion of all types of wisdom; second, a discussion of wisdom in relation to its objects.
Wisdom in its general sense is sixfold:
First, enumeration;
second, categories;
third, characteristics.
Fourth, illumination;
fifth, discernment;
sixth, opening.
Regarding "calculation" (gaṇanā): first, mundane knowledge;
second, the knowledge of the four foundations of mindfulness during the five stages of settling the mind.
3. The wisdom of the four roots of goodness;
4. The wisdom of the four fruits;
5. The wisdom of the pratyekabuddha.
Sixth, the wisdom of the six perfections;
seventh, the wisdom of the śrāvakas who realize the nature of phenomena;
eighth, the wisdom of the pratyekabuddhas who realize the nature of phenomena.
9. The wisdom of the bodhisattva who realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) entering the true skillful means;
10. The wisdom of the bodhisattva who realizes the nature of phenomena emerging into the provisional;
11. The wisdom of the ten stages of faith in the Separate Teaching (prthaktīya).
12. The knowledge of the thirty minds.
13. The knowledge of the ten stages.
14. The Buddha-knowledge of the Three Piṭakas.
15. The Buddha-wisdom of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
16. The Buddha-wisdom of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
17. The wisdom of the disciples of the Five Grades (Wupin) in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
18. Wisdom of the purification of the six sense faculties;
19. Wisdom from the first stage up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment;
20. Wisdom of Sublime Enlightenment.

Second, regarding their categories: mundane wisdom lacks the Path and consists of false calculations and deluded attachments; its mental activities lie outside of principle, and because it neither believes nor enters [the truth], it constitutes one category.

The five stages of settling the mind and the four foundations of mindfulness have already entered the initial stage of the Worthy (ārya) and possess the fragrance of the Buddha-dharma; as both are still external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana), they constitute another category.
The four roots of goodness are grouped as one because they are equally mundane noble ones (pṛthagjana).
The four fruits are grouped as one because they equally realize the ultimate truth.
The Pratyekabuddhas are grouped as one because their contemplation of specific characteristics is capable of eradicating habitual tendencies (vāsanā).
In the Six Perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), the wisdom that takes principles as its object is weak while the wisdom that takes phenomena as its object is strong; therefore, they are treated as one.
In the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇanaya), the śrāvakas of the skillful means possess superior wisdom regarding the nature of dharmas; therefore, they are treated as one.
The Pratyekabuddhas are slightly superior [to the Śrāvakas], and thus constitute one category.
The Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) who enter the true [nature] through the wisdom of skillful means study all four gates, and thus constitute one category.
The Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who emerge into the provisional (chujia) possess wisdom that correctly takes the conventional as its object, and thus constitute one category.

Regarding the wisdom of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*): because one first realizes the Middle Way, it is superior to what precedes and inferior to what follows; thus, they are treated as one.
Furthermore, the thirty minds (*triṃśaccitta*) of the Separate Teaching are all considered internal ordinary beings (*adhyātma-prthagjana*); thus, they are treated as one.
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are identical in being noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), and thus constitute one.
The Buddha of the Tripiṭaka is designated by the title of "Teacher" (*śāstṛ*), and as he surpasses the disciples of the three vehicles, he constitutes one.
The Buddha-wisdom of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*) excels in severing delusions and illuminating the capacities of beings, and thus it constitutes one.
The Buddha-wisdom of the Separate Teaching is further superior, and thus constitutes one [category].

In the Perfect Teaching, the disciples of the five grades all equally possess the nature of afflictions, yet they are able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata; therefore, this constitutes one [category].
The wisdom of the purification of the six sense organs is proximate to the ultimate truth, and is therefore counted as one.
From the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāyogi-bodhi*), they equally destroy ignorance (*avidyā*), and are therefore counted as one.
The Buddha-wisdom of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is unsurpassed and most venerable, and is therefore counted as one.
Thus, according to their respective categories, those that are similar are either separated or combined and judged to be twenty, and so forth. Third, regarding the discernment of characteristics:
the worldly wisdom of India reaches its ultimate limit at the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

What is revered here consists primarily of loyalty and filial piety, the Five Constants, the Six Arts, astronomy, geography, medical prescriptions, divination and physiognomy, military strategy, and methods of commerce; one must recognize a thousand species of plants and know the names of ten thousand varieties of birds and beasts.
Furthermore, he smeared his left side and cut his right side without feeling either hatred or love.

Having attained the fundamental dhyānas, he manifested the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*): he caused rivers to stand still at his ear, transformed Śakra into a sheep, swallowed up wind and clouds, and reached out to touch the sun and moon.
The Dharma is a worldly dharma; concentration is immovable concentration, and wisdom is the emergence from immovability.
To seek fame and profit and to increase views and craving is what is known by the worldly mind; therefore, it is called "worldly wisdom."

Regarding the five cessations and the four foundations of mindfulness: they are called "cessations" because they possess concentration (*samādhi*), and they are called "contemplations" because they possess wisdom (*prajñā*).
Contemplation can overturn the perverse, while concentration can restrain the distracted.

Counting the breath remedies distraction; the foul (impurity) remedies greed; compassion remedies anger; dependent origination remedies delusion; and mindfulness of the Buddha remedies obstacles to the Path.
The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) consist of the four types of wisdom that contemplate the Truth of Suffering, serving as the remedy for the four inversions (viparyāsa).
Because these four contemplations prevent the arising of the four inversions, they first overturn them;
yet, as one has not yet entered the principle of the Noble Ones (ārya), they are termed the "wisdom of the external ordinary person" (bāhyapṛthagjana-jñāna).

The Dharma of Heat (*uṣmagata*) gives rise to wisdom by taking the four noble truths as its object; it subdues the afflictions, and as this wisdom further increases, it becomes the sixteen moments of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
It is like a fire-drill: when the upper and lower parts rely upon one another, fire is produced to burn the wood.
Because one possesses wisdom that knows there is an object, it can generate the "warmth" of knowledge, which causes existence to wither.
It is like a heap of flowers gathered in summer; as the flowers produce warmth, they themselves wither away.

Furthermore, by relying on the aggregates (*skandha*) and contemplating the aggregates, one kindles the fire of wisdom, which in turn burns away the aggregates—just as when two bamboo sticks are rubbed together to produce fire, the resulting fire consumes the bamboo grove itself.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
"In seeking the fire of wisdom for liberation, 'warmth' (*uṣmagata*) is foremost."
Just as fire is characterized by smoke appearing first,
so too the fire of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is characterized by the factor of warmth (*uṣmagata*) appearing first.
Just as the sun is characterized by the appearance of light at its beginning, it is therefore called "warmth."

One who develops faith in the True Dharma and Vinaya and cherishes the True Dharma takes the Truth of the Path as their object; one who believes in the Vinaya takes the Truth of Cessation as their object.
Since the stage of "Heat" that possesses faith can take all four truths as its objects, why do you say there are only two?
Answer: These two are most excellent and should be explained first.
Furthermore, the True Dharma consists of the three truths, while the Vinaya is the truth of cessation.
As the Buddha said to Pūrṇamāsa:
"I have a teaching in four statements that I shall speak for you; do you wish to know it?
You may ask as you please."
The four lines refer to the Four Noble Truths.
The intention is that all acts of giving and maintaining the precepts are directed toward liberation.
The arising of the meditative concentration of the form realm is its basis.
The previously arisen wholesome roots within one’s own stage (*svabhūmi*) are the similar causes and conditions (*sabhāga-pratyaya*).
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) are their fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The subsequently arisen wholesome roots, which are similar to those of one’s own stage, are the fruit of reliance (*adhipati-phala*).
The five aggregates of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are its retribution (*vipāka*).
Nirvāṇa is its definitive cause, and the non-severance of the roots of goodness is its benefit.
The sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) are its practice; it is dependently originated and constitutes cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
The three samādhis bound to the realm of form correspond to the three faculties as previously explained; when many minds are associated with these, it is a state of regression.
There are three grades of "Heat" (ūṣmagata):
namely, the lowest-of-the-low, the middle-of-the-low, and the highest-of-the-low.
The stage of "Summits" (mūrdhan) has three levels: medium-low, medium-middle, and medium-high.
The stage of "Patience" (kṣānti) has two types:
The lower-upper and the upper-middle.
The Supreme Worldly Dharma has one type:
namely, the upper-upper.

Regarding these four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in terms of three grades: *uṣmagata* (Heat) is the lower, *mūrdhan* (Summit) is the middle, and *kṣānti* (Patience) and *laukikāgradharma* (Supreme Mundane Dharma) are the upper.
Furthermore, there are those who say that *uṣmagata* is twofold:
These refer to the lower-lower and the lower-middle.
There are three types of "summits" (mūrdhan):
namely, the lower-upper, the middle-lower, and the middle-middle.
There are three types of patience (*kṣānti*):
namely, medium-superior, superior-inferior, and superior-medium.
There is one type of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

That is to say, they are categorized as "superior-superior. Furthermore, expressed in terms of three grades: "Heat" (ūṣmagata) is the lowest-lowest; "Summit" (mūrdhan) is the middle-lowest; "Patience" (kṣānti) is the upper-middle; and the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) is the superior-superior.
Guṣa said: "The stage of Heat (uṣmagata) has three levels, while the stage of Summits (mūrdhan) has six:
from the lowest-of-the-low up to the middle-of-the-high."
There are eight levels of patience (*kṣānti*),
ranging from the lowest-of-the-low to the upper-middle;
the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is exclusively the highest-of-the-high.
Speaking in terms of three grades: the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) is of one kind, namely the lower;
the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*) is of two kinds, namely the lower and the middle;
the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) is of three kinds, namely the lower, the middle, and the upper.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma has one type, namely the "superior.
Regarding the Heat stage, there are two types of relinquishment:
first, relinquishing by changing the realm or level; second, relinquishing at the time of falling back.
When regressing, one abandons them; when falling into hell and committing the five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), one does not sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
The same applies to the *mūrdhan* (Summits).
For the *kṣānti* (Patience), there is only the single abandonment [of the roots of goodness], and one does not fall into hell, and so forth.

The "Dharma of the Summit" consists of the wholesome roots of the form realm, which are characterized by being mobile or immobile, abiding or non-abiding, difficult or not difficult, subject to severance or not subject to severance, and liable to regression or not liable to regression.
Regarding those who are "mobile" up to "regressive," there are two types:
the lower is *uṣmagata* (Heat), and the higher is *mūrdhan* (Summit).
Those who are "immovable" up to "non-regressive" are also of two types:
The lower [stage] is patience (*kṣānti*), and the upper is the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Furthermore, there are those who say it should be called the "lower summit" (*mūrdhan*); why is this so?
It is called "Summit" (mūrdhan) because it stands at the peak of the stage of Heat (uṣmagata).
It is called "Lower" (adhas) because it is situated below the stage of Patience (kṣānti).
Furthermore, some say that it is like a path on a mountain summit where a person does not remain for long.
If no obstacles arise, one will certainly pass beyond this stage and reach that;
if obstacles are encountered, one will immediately retreat.
The practitioner does not remain at the summit for long; if no obstacles arise, they will certainly reach the stage of patience (kṣānti).
If one encounters difficulties and regresses, one returns to the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
Because it is like the summit of a mountain, it is called "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).
What is its contemplation?
One gives rise to a slight and inferior faith toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
This faith is called "slight and inferior" because this Dharma will not remain for long; thus it is termed "inferior.
This faith arises with the Buddha as its object and constitutes a slight faith; it takes the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) as its condition.
The arising of inferior faith conditioned by phenomena is conditioned by the truth of cessation.
Question:
Since it should be able to take all four truths as its object, why is it said to be conditioned by two truths?
Answer: Because the Path and Cessation are superior.
Being pure and faultless, they are sublime and detached.
It is a ground capable of generating faith, for the purpose of producing a mind of faith and delight in those who are to be transformed.
If the World-Honored One were to teach that suffering and its origin are objects to be trusted and revered, then there would be no one to be transformed.
How can these afflictions, misdeeds, wrong views, and perversions be worthy of respect or faith?
I am constantly oppressed by them.
Those to be converted feel joy toward the Path and Cessation; for this reason, two [aspects] are taught.

Furthermore, there are those who say that faith in the Buddha and the Sangha is the path as a condition, while faith in the Dharma is the condition for the three truths; thus, one completely believes in the four truths.
Question:
One who dwells at the "summit" (mūrdhan) also has faith in the aggregates (skandhas), faith in the Jewels (ratna), and faith in the truths (satya).
Why is it that one speaks only of faith in the Three Jewels?
Answer: The Three Jewels are the objects that give rise to faith and reverence.
When one experiences a sense of joy and satisfaction regarding the aggregates (skandhas) according to the practitioner's inclination, this is called "Heat" (ūṣmagata).
When one experiences a sense of joy and satisfaction regarding the [Three] Jewels, this is called "Summit" (mūrdhan).
When one experiences a sense of joy and satisfaction regarding the Truths (satya), this is called "Patience" (kṣānti).
Question:
For what reason is falling back from the *mūrdhan* (summit) mentioned, while falling back from the *uṣmagata* (heat) is not? Answer:
Since there is falling back from the *mūrdhan* (Summits), one should likewise speak of falling back from *uṣmagata* (Heat).
When the practitioner is at the stage of the Summits, many afflictions and karmic obstacles arise.
These afflictions and so forth form this thought:
If the practitioner reaches the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), [the practitioner] further considers: "In whose body shall I produce the retribution?
When departing from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [the practitioner] likewise reflects:
"The practitioner has emerged from the desire realm; in whose body shall I produce the retribution?"
When departing from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one also reflects:
"Once the practitioner has abandoned desire for that state, they will no longer receive a body; in whose body, then, shall I again produce the fruit of retribution?"
During these three periods, there are many obstacles.
Because these obstacles cause one to regress, there is great distress and affliction.
It is like a person who sees a treasure trove and rejoices greatly, yet loses it just as they wish to take it.
One who dwells in the stage of the Summit reflects:
"Before long, I shall attain Patience, forever severing the evil realms and obtaining great and profound benefit, just like the Noble Ones.
Yet, suddenly falling back and losing [this state], they experience great distress and affliction; therefore, it is called "retrogression from the Summit."

If one can draw near to virtuous friends and hear from them the Dharma of expedient means that accords with reality, observing it correctly within the mind, and thus believe in the Buddha’s bodhi, believe in the well-expounded Dharma, and believe in the pure merits of the Sangha—this is called the Jewel of Faith.
To speak of the impermanence of form, up to and including the impermanence of consciousness, is called faith in the aggregates (*skandha*).
To know that there is suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, is called faith in the truths (*satya*).
If one abides in this manner, one dwells at the summit; if one does not abide in this manner, one falls back from the summit.

Regarding the contemplation of the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), one correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the suffering of the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).
The accumulation of formations of the desire realm, and the accumulation of formations of the form and formless realms.
The cessation of formations of the desire realm, and the cessation of formations of the form and formless realms.
The path leading to the abandonment of formations of the desire realm, and the path leading to the abandonment of formations of the form and formless realms.
These thirty-two moments of mind are termed "lower patience" (mṛdu-kṣānti).

At a later time, the practitioner gradually reduces the mental applications (prayoga) and their objects (ālambana), and again correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, the suffering of the form realm, and the formless realm, up to contemplating the path that abandons the desire realm—excluding the contemplation of the path that abandons the form and formless realms. From this point onward, it is termed "middle patience" (madhya-kṣānti).

Furthermore, one again correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, contemplates the suffering of the form and formless realms, and even contemplates the cessation of formations in the form and formless realms, thereby eliminating all paths.

Furthermore, one correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm and the suffering of the form and formless realms, and so on, up to contemplating the cessation of formations in the desire realm, excluding the cessation of formations in the form and formless realms.

Furthermore, one correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, and so on, up to contemplating the origination of formations in the form and formless realms, thereby eliminating all cessation.

Again, one correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, and so on, up to contemplating the origination of formations in the desire realm, thereby eliminating the origination of formations in the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, one correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, and eliminates all origins [of suffering].
Furthermore, one correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, and eliminates the suffering of the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, one correctly contemplates the desire realm as permanent, continuous, and uninterrupted, without distancing oneself from it.

When contemplating in this manner, a profound sense of weary revulsion arises, and [the afflictions] are further diminished; one then applies two moments of mind to contemplate a single practice, similar to the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma (*dharma-jñāna*).
To contemplate correctly in this manner is called "middle patience" (*madhyamā kṣānti*).
Furthermore, to contemplate the suffering of the desire realm with a single-minded focus is called "superior patience" (*adhimātrā kṣānti*).

Next, one gives rise to the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*); following the supreme mundane dharma, the "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises next.
It is like a person who wishes to travel from his own country to another; possessing great wealth, he cannot carry it all with him, so he exchanges goods for money.
Still dissatisfied with the money, he exchanges it for gold;
still dissatisfied with the gold, he exchanges it for precious gems of high value, and then departs for the other country.
The practitioner gradually abandons [the objects of meditation] until, through an uninterrupted continuity, they give rise to superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
Following superior patience, the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) arises.
Following the supreme mundane dharma, the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) arises.
Question:
Are there three grades of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)?
Answer: [There are.]
One person lacks it, while many possess it.
Śāriputra is superior, Maudgalyāyana is middling, and all others are inferior.
When categorized according to Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas, they form three grades.

Regarding the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*): these mental states and their associated factors are the most excellent, the most superior, the longest-lasting, the most venerable, the highest, and the most sublime among all other dharmas.
It is both partial and total.
"Partial" refers to the superior mundane dharmas (*laukika-agra-dharma*), which do not surpass the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).

This is because the retinue of the vision of the truths is inseparable from them, because the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) predominates therein, and because the cultivation of dhyāna does not arise in the same place as that of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
At the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), because all roots of goodness are forever free from all stains and obstructions,
how could the three samādhis— even up to the contemptible outflow-free states— not be entirely superior, let alone the outflowing states?

The stages of Heat (ūṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), and Patience (kṣānti) are also superior; they should be called "foremost" and "superior. They are superior to the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), immeasurables (apramāṇa), liberations (vimokṣa), and spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) attained by all ordinary persons (pṛthagjana).
Some say it is "supremely superior," but this does not mean it is superior among all worldly undertakings; rather, it is because it can open the gateway to the Noble Path.

Those factors such as the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) cannot open the gateway to the Noble Path; it is the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) that opens the gateway to the Noble Path. While those factors such as the vision of the truths obtain the cultivation of the factors for seeing the truths and so forth, [the Supreme Mundane Dharma alone opens the path].
That which is attained through cultivation is entirely the functional efficacy of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Regarding the meaning of the term "Supreme Mundane Dharma": the sense of being most excellent is the "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*);
attaining the sublime fruit is the ultimate meaning. It is like the pinnacle of a high banner, beyond which there is nothing higher; thus it is the ultimate meaning.
Question:
Are there distinctions among the various meanings mentioned previously? Answer:
All of these are praises of the supreme and wondrous meaning, yet they also possess distinctions:

it is called "supreme" (*parama*) in relation to impurity and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*); "excellent" (*viśiṣṭa*) in relation to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); "vast" (*udāra*) in relation to the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); "venerable" (*agra*) in relation to the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*); "superior" (*uttama*) in relation to the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*); and "wondrous" (*praṇīta*) in relation to the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*).

Furthermore, based on the *anāgamya* stage it is supreme; based on the first dhyāna it is excellent; the intermediate state is extensive; the second dhyāna is honorable; the third dhyāna is superior; and the fourth dhyāna is sublime.
These various explanations are based on the commentary of the *Vibhāṣā*; those who wish to know them in detail should consult that work.
Regarding the first fruit, there are eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*).
The three fruits involve heavy contemplation of the Truth, consisting of the nine unimpeded knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*) and the nine liberating knowledges (*vimukti-jñāna*).

The Pratyekabuddha employs both general and specific characteristics; for instance, when clarifying suffering and its origin across the three periods of time and analyzing the twelve links of dependent origination, this constitutes the aspect of specific characteristics.
In the six perfections, the wisdom of principle is weak and thus merely suppresses afflictions without severing them;
the wisdom of phenomena is strong, enabling one to relinquish body, life, and wealth without any lingering attachment.
Even when Śrāvakas have attained the truth and become sages, they still speak of "my robe" and "my bowl," and debate matters such as their relative strengths and weaknesses.
The śrāvakas of the Shared Teaching, through the single gate of general characteristics, realize that the conventional is itself the ultimate.
The pratyekabuddhas of the Shared Teaching are able, within the gates of both general and specific characteristics, to realize that the conventional is itself the ultimate.

The Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching are able, through the four gates, to realize that conventional phenomena—both in their general and specific characteristics—are identical to the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, they are able to universally emerge into the provisional realm via these four gates to teach and transform sentient beings.
The ten levels of faith involve believing in the true suchness and real mark at the summit of the fruits; seeking this principle, one gives rise to the ten levels of faith.
The ten abidings involve correctly practicing the entry into emptiness, while concurrently practicing the provisional and the middle.
In the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*), one primarily practices the conventional (*prajñapti*) and secondarily practices the middle way (*madhyama*).
In the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), one primarily practices the middle way. In the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one realizes the middle way.
From the second bhūmi upward, one deliberates repeatedly within this process.
A Buddha of the Tripiṭaka, in a single moment, employs thirty-four moments of mind—
namely, eight patiences, eight knowledges, nine unimpeded knowledges, and nine liberations— to exhaustively sever both the primary afflictions and their residual habits.

In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the Buddha sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and, through the wisdom of a single thought-moment of resonance, severs the remaining residual habitual tendencies.
In the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), the Buddha employs the final moment of mind after the diamond-like samādhi to sever the last grade of ignorance, thereby attaining ultimate Buddhahood.
Some say: "The moment of abandonment is perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
The Buddha has nothing to abandon; he simply realizes and attains the fulfillment of complete enlightenment."

Having perfected the five grades [of the Ten Abidings], one does not sever the five desires yet purifies the six sense faculties; though possessing the nature of afflictions, one is able to know the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
At the stage of the purification of the six faculties, one attains the semblance of the wisdom of the Middle Way.
In the first dwelling, one attains the Tathāgata’s single body that is immeasurable bodies, entering the ocean of the flow of Dharma where one proceeds with effortless spontaneity.
The subsequent stages are self-evident and need not be recorded further.

Fourth, regarding "the luminous wisdom that illuminates objects": if one holds that wisdom illuminates objects or that objects give rise to wisdom, all four permutations fall into the trap of substantiality (*svabhāva*), as explained at length in the *Pṛthak-vyākhyā* (Separate Record) and other sources.
If realms and wisdom are established through the causal conditions of the four *siddhāntas*, they exist merely as names and so forth.
Question:
While wisdom can illuminate the realm, can the realm also illuminate wisdom?
Answer: If one provides an interpretation based on the inconceivable (*acintya*), they mutually illuminate one another, and there is no impediment to the meaning.
As the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"To speak of wisdom and the locus of wisdom, both are termed *prajñā*.
It is like the surfaces of mirrors reflecting one another, or as the single great earth is able to produce various sprouts, and those sprouts likewise arise from the single earth."
Setting aside this point for now:
mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*) illuminates the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*) of the six destinies;

the five stopping-and-contemplating minds (*pañca-sthāpanā-citta*) proceed to the essence of dharmas; these constitute seven types of wisdom that illuminate the ten suchnesses of the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*).

The wisdom of the Bodhisattvas who emerge from the provisional teachings through the six perfections and the supernatural powers belongs to both categories: it illuminates the ten suchnesses of the Bodhisattvas in their upward seeking, and it illuminates the ten suchnesses of the six realms in their downward transformation.
The forty mental wisdoms also belong to both categories:
they illuminate the ten suchnesses of the Bodhisattvas in their upward seeking, and they illuminate the ten suchnesses of the six realms in their downward transformation.
The wisdom of the ten stages belongs to both categories: when it illuminates sequentially, it illuminates the ten suchnesses of the bodhisattvas;
when it illuminates non-sequentially, it illuminates the ten suchnesses of the Buddhas.
Beyond the five stages, there are four types of wisdom, all of which illuminate the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm.
The summary is as follows; for a detailed analysis, and so forth:

regarding the twenty knowledges that illuminate the four types of twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), there are seven knowledges—namely, worldly knowledge, the five cessations (*pañca-vinodana*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], up to the pratyekabuddha, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka—which illuminate the twelvefold dependent origination of birth and death within the realm of the conceivable (*saṃcintya*).

The Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) comprises five types of wisdom: the wisdom of the skillful means for the three vehicles entering the truth, the wisdom of emerging into the conventional, and the Buddha-wisdom; these collectively illumine the realm of the twelve links of dependent origination, which is inconceivable, neither arising nor ceasing.

The four stages of the Separate Teaching—the ten levels of faith, the thirty minds, the ten grounds, and Buddhahood—possess four types of wisdom that illumine the inconceivable realm of the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Within these, there are certainly distinct nuances; however, for now, we shall proceed according to the general classification.
The four wisdoms of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) illuminate the inconceivable realm of the twelve links of dependent origination, which is neither arising nor ceasing.

Regarding the twenty wisdoms that illuminate the four types of Four Noble Truths: the aforementioned seven wisdoms, such as those of the Tripitaka (Sanzang), illuminate the realm of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing.
Next, the five wisdoms of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) illuminate the realm of the four truths of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Next, the four wisdoms of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) illuminate the realm of the immeasurable four truths.
Next, the four wisdoms of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) illuminate the realm of the unconditioned four truths.
Next, regarding the twenty knowledges that illuminate the two truths: the first seven knowledges are those that illuminate the two truths of analytical emptiness (*vibhāga-śūnyatā*);
the subsequent five knowledges are those that illuminate the two truths of essential emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Next, regarding the two truths as illuminated and manifested by the eight knowledges (*jñāna*):
the distinctions between the Separate (*bie*) and Perfect (*yuan*) teachings and their mutual interpenetration can be understood through reflection, and so forth.

Next, concerning the illumination of the three truths by twenty knowledges: first, the seven knowledges that illuminate the two truths within non-existence refer to phenomena produced by causes and conditions, all of which are subsumed under the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Next, the five wisdoms that illuminate the two truths within the implicit [teaching]—namely, the single phrase "emptiness"—are all subsumed under the truth of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).

Next, the eight wisdoms of the Separate and Perfect [vehicles] that illuminate the two truths within the explicit [teaching]—namely, "provisional names," which are also called the Middle Way—are both subsumed under the truth of the middle way (*madhyamā-satya*).

Next, regarding the twenty kinds of wisdom that illuminate the single ultimate truth (*ekābhisamaya-satya*): this must be explained by citing the *Vyākhyāyukti*, which clarifies that all four *siddhāntas* are called "truth.
They are real from the perspective of the worldly convention (*loka*), and so on, up to being real from the perspective of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).

One should know that truthful speech also pervades the Four Noble Truths: it is real because of arising and ceasing; it is real because of the absence of arising and ceasing; it is real because of being immeasurable; and it is real because of being unconditioned.
First, the seven wisdoms of the Tripiṭaka illuminate the reality of arising and ceasing.
Next, the five wisdoms of the Shared Teaching illuminate the reality of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Next, the four wisdoms of the Distinct Teaching illuminate the reality of the immeasurable.
Next, the four wisdoms of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) illuminate the reality of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*).
Regarding the various realities mentioned previously, and so forth:

next, as for the statement that the twenty wisdoms have neither truth nor illumination—there is no distinct principle of "no truth. If one attains awakening regarding the four kinds of Four Noble Truths, one no longer perceives either truth or non-truth; therefore, "no truth" is also universally applicable.
First, the seven wisdoms illuminate the truth of non-arising regarding arising and ceasing, because the arising of arising cannot be described.
Next, the five wisdoms illuminate the truth of non-arising regarding non-arising and non-ceasing, because the arising of non-arising cannot be described.
Next, the four wisdoms illuminate the truth of non-existence (wu-di), because that which is not born cannot be said to be born.
Next, the four wisdoms illuminate the truth of non-action (wu-zuo), because that which is not born cannot be said to be born.
The absence of truth in the former [teaching] is provisional, while the absence of truth in the latter is ultimate; this is according to verbal instruction.

If one proceeds from the perspective of wondrous awakening, which is identical to what is illuminated within the minds of the sages, then no distinction between the provisional and the ultimate is perceived; therefore, it is neither provisional nor ultimate.
An empty fist deceives small children; [the Buddha] uses this to entice and deliver all beings.
Through skillful means he speaks of the provisional, and through skillful means he speaks of the real.
When one realizes the underlying principle, there is no longer provisional or real; therefore, that which is neither provisional nor real is called "sublime" (miao).
Fifth, regarding the clarification of the coarse and the subtle: the first twelve instances of wisdom are coarse, while the latter eight instances of wisdom are subtle.

Why is this? The Buddhas of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) vehicles are themselves impermanent and do not preach permanence; how then could those of the two vehicles or the bodhisattvas hear of permanence, believe in permanence, or cultivate permanence?
Therefore, it is considered coarse.

In the Separate Teaching (*pṛthagdeśanā*), one hears of the eternal at the very beginning of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*); since even the faith and cultivation regarding the eternal surpass those Buddhas, how much more so the others?
Therefore, it is considered sublime.
As is commonly said:
"The fact that the *Lotus Sūtra* does not clarify the eternal is merely the perspective of the Tripiṭaka."
Now, it is clarified that within the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), one has already transcended the Sage; thus, the eight stages [of the ten abidings] constitute the "wondrous.
Furthermore, regarding the four wisdoms of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna* or *vyatireka-śāsana*), three are coarse and one is wondrous.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), all four wisdoms are termed "wondrous.
Why is this? As the followers of the *Dicheng* (Earth-Teaching) school say:
"The Middle Way is that which can be fully manifested only at the stage of fruition; for a beginner to look up with faith toward this principle is like a mountain suspended by a lotus fiber.
Therefore, it is said that both faith and practice are not yet of the Perfect (or Complete) meaning.
Therefore, the wisdom of the ten stages of faith is coarse.
In the ten abodes, one primarily cultivates emptiness while incidentally cultivating the provisional and the middle.
In the ten practices, one primarily cultivates the provisional while incidentally cultivating the middle.
At the beginning of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), one first correctly practices;
herein there is only principle (*li*), but not the full array of dharmas, and for this reason they are all coarse.
When the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*) ascends, it shatters ignorance and perceives the Middle Way; when realized, it becomes sublime.
It is like the case of the *Vaipulya* (Mahāyāna) and *Tripiṭaka* (Hīnayāna) schools: both attain the Way, yet the gate of the Tripiṭaka is clumsy.
Now, the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*) is likewise; while its teaching gates are all provisional, its realization is wondrous, and so forth.

Regarding the fact that all four wisdoms in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) are sublime: as explained in the Dharma-characteristics (Faxiang), one believes according to what is taught and practices according to the principle. Beginning with the five grades and culminating in Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue), these are real rather than provisional; therefore, they are all sublime.
This is called explaining "sublime wisdom" by way of depending upon "coarse wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the coarse and the sublime in terms of knowledge (*jñāna*) and vision (*darśana*), what are knowledge and vision?
There are, however, four types of analysis:
"Not knowing and not seeing," "knowing but not seeing," "seeing but not knowing," and "both knowing and seeing.
First, these are explained according to the Tripiṭaka; second, they are explained according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuan); the intermediate cases may be understood by analogy.
Ordinary persons do not know because they have not heard [the teaching], and they do not see because they have not realized it.

From the five cessations (pañca-nivaraṇa-viśrāma) and the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) up to the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma), one knows because of having heard it, but it is not seeing because it has not yet been realized.
Because the Pratyekabuddha does not hear [the teachings], it is not "knowledge"; because he realizes it spontaneously, it is "vision.
Because the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] involve hearing, they are also "knowledge," and because they involve realization, they are also "vision."
The distinction between the coarse and the subtle according to the various schools can be understood.

To explain this according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): because the seven stages of expedient means have not heard [the Dharma], they do not know it; because they have not yet realized it, they do not see it.
The five grades and the six faculties know through hearing, yet they do not see because they have not yet realized [the truth].
Those who awaken their latent predispositions (vāsanā) are said to "see," for they do not rely on hearing and thus do not [merely] "know."
Those who receive the teaching and realize entry also know and see.
These successive stages are transmitted as being coarse or subtle;
yet, when discussed from the ultimate perspective, the twenty kinds of wisdom mentioned previously can, in brief, be subsumed within no more than two types: provisional and real wisdom.
As the sutra states:
"The Tathāgata’s skillful means, knowledge, vision, and pāramitās are all fully perfected. This summarizes and consolidates all the various provisional wisdoms mentioned previously.
“The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound” summarizes the aforementioned true wisdom (bhūta-jñāna).
Since his skillful means (upāya) are fully perfected, what is there that they do not encompass?
Since his knowledge and vision are thus vast and profound, what is there that they do not encompass?
The depths of the objective realm are boundless, and the waters of wisdom cannot be fathomed; only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively penetrate them.
Such knowledge and vision constitute the eye and wisdom.
The eye is the fulfillment of the five eyes; wisdom is the three knowledges within a single mind.
The knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) knows the ultimate reality, while the two knowledges know the provisional means.
The Buddha-eye perceives the ultimate reality (*tattva*), while the four eyes perceive the provisional (*upāya*).
This knowledge is itself vision, and this vision is itself knowledge.
Compared to the various forms of wisdom mentioned previously, those wisdoms are coarse; this knowledge and vision is termed "sublime" (*praṇīta*).
If one understands the meaning within this knowledge and vision, there is no further need to discuss the five eyes.
Those who are deluded have not yet attained clarity; therefore, we shall again distinguish between the coarse and the subtle regarding the eyes.
For instance, if the physical eye is blind and closed, by what means could one perceive forms?
To merely hear others speak and give rise to various conceptions is ultimately not true insight.
If you wish to open your eyes, you must treat the cataracts; what benefit is there in keeping your eyes closed and clinging to contention?
To imagine with eyes closed is coarse; to see with eyes open is subtle.

When the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) has not yet opened, one does not see what lies beyond obstructions, which is considered coarse; however, through the power of cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), vows, and wisdom (*jñāna*), one can produce pure form (*rūpa*) that penetrates both inside and outside of obstructions, such that there is no separation between light and darkness.
When the eye of wisdom has not yet opened, one constantly traverses the path of death; even if one's thoughts and perceptions exist, they are nonetheless unreal and thus termed "coarse.
When the untainted [wisdom] dawns with clarity, it is therefore called "sublime."
Because the principle of the Truths is clearly understood, it is called "sublime.
When the Dharma-eye has not yet opened, one preaches the Dharma according to differing capacities;
for example, Śāriputra’s biased teaching and Pūrṇa’s treatment of those who are like foul vessels are termed "coarse."
To break through hindrances and penetrate non-knowledge, and to discern the medicine and the illness—this is called "wondrous.
If the Buddha-eye is not opened, one does not perceive the true mark (dharmatā).
Therefore, the text says:
"Because it cannot be known by those of the two vehicles, nor by those who have newly resolved their minds, nor by non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, all four eyes are coarse.

Excluding those among the assembly of bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm—who enter through faith and, resembling the Buddha-eye, can open the true Buddha’s knowledge and vision—it is only then called 'sublime.'"
Most teachings speak of the four eyes, or describe the Buddha-eye by including it within the four; therefore, they are considered coarse.
This present sutra speaks exclusively of the Buddha-eye; therefore, it is considered sublime.
This refers to regarding the coarse as the sublime.
Sixth, clarifying the opening of the coarse to reveal the sublime: if the sixteen preceding instances of wisdom are not decisively realized, they are merely coarse wisdom;
if they are decisively realized, they all become sublime wisdom.

Why is this? It is like King Wonderful Adornment, who was formerly a heterodox practitioner with worldly wisdom; upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he immediately attained definitive understanding. By means of false appearances entering into correct appearances, he cultivated the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without being moved by various views, and entered the eightfold noble path without abandoning the eight heterodoxies. This is precisely the resolution of worldly wisdom to attain entry into sublime wisdom.

It may be equal to the five stages, or equal to the stage of semblance, or equal to the stage of partial attainment; there is entry at each successive stage, and the meaning is subtle, as explained at length.

If the wisdom of the five methods of cessation (*pañca-vinodana-upāya*) up to the wisdom of the Buddhas of the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*) is not decisively realized, it is considered coarse wisdom.
Now, with the provisional being opened to reveal the real, [the Buddha says], "That which you practice is the Bodhisattva path," thereby causing them to enter the sublime stage.

One must, one by one, bring forth the twelvefold wisdoms to enter the perfect and wondrous four wisdoms—or, as the case may be, the five grades, the stage of semblance, the stage of partial attainment, and so forth.
Furthermore, one decisively realizes that the distinct wisdom of the Separate Teaching enters into the wondrous wisdom (*miào zhì*).
One should understand that its very essence is a specific stage (*bì*), entering into that specific stage through subtle discernment, and so forth.
The sixteen coarse knowledges all become sublime knowledges; since there is no longer any coarseness to be contrasted with, this is the sublimity of knowledge that transcends all relativity.

Furthermore, regarding the opening of the coarse eye to become the sublime eye: although other sutras speak of five eyes, these five eyes are not integrated, and for this reason they are considered coarse.
This sutra now definitively resolves the four eyes, causing one to enter the Buddha-eye.
The text says:
"The eyes born of one's parents shall thereby attain purity."
"One who studies the Mahāyāna, although possessing only the fleshly eye, is said to possess the Buddha-eye.
This means that the fleshly eye, when decisively realized, is called the Buddha-eye.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"Who in the world possesses true divine vision? There is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who perceives all Buddha-lands without relying on dualistic characteristics.
This is precisely the definitive realization of divine vision; it is the Buddha-eye.
"May I obtain the foremost purity of the wisdom-eye like that of the World-Honored One" refers to the definitive realization of the wisdom-eye, which enables one to enter the sublime.
As for the definitive realization of the dharma-eye to enter the sublime, it is the fulfillment of the knowledge of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭi-jñāna*).
The four eyes merge into the Buddha-eye, which is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; thus the text says:
"The definitive understanding of the Śrāvaka-dharma is the king of all sutras.
When the five eyes are fully perfected, one achieves Bodhi and opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, it is called "wondrous."
Question:
It is only when the Buddha-eye is opened that it is called "wondrous.
Although the six sense organs may be pure, why are they not considered wondrous?
Answer: Although the Buddha-eye has not yet opened, one is already able to achieve perfect study and perfect faith.

It is like the kalaviṅka bird; although still within its shell, its song already surpasses that of all other birds. This refers to the provisional name, the semblance, and so forth, which are all wondrous.
If it is opened, this refers to the "excellent" and the "ultimately excellent," and so forth.
Second, the clear wisdom regarding objects has two parts:
first, regarding the five sense objects; second, regarding the mutual illumination of objects.

First, regarding the correspondence with the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*): since this is the purport of the sutra and is explained throughout, it can be understood on its own; therefore, it will not be further explicated here.
Second, regarding the wisdom that corresponds to the four kinds of twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"There are four ways of contemplating the twelvefold dependent origination."
By observing with inferior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;
by observing with middling wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
and by observing with superior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a bodhisattva.
"Because of contemplation with the highest of high wisdom, one attains the Bodhi of the Buddha. Why is this?
The twelve links of dependent origination are fundamentally a single realm; however, because the understanding of these conditions differs, it unfolds into four types.
Now, I shall explain this according to the intent of the four teachings:

the Tripitaka contains three types of practitioners, all of whom take the analytical wisdom that contemplates the phenomena of the twelve links of dependent origination within the realm of desire as their initial gateway.
However, their analytical wisdom is shallow and weak; among the three types of practitioners, the śrāvakas are the most inferior.
Because they employ a shallow teaching for inferior persons, it is termed "inferior wisdom" (hīna-jñāna).

The Shared Teaching (pāṭha-sāmānya) also comprises three types of persons who likewise use essential wisdom to contemplate the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination within the realm of desire. Although their realization of the nature of phenomena is profound when compared to the Śrāvaka Vehicle, it is not yet skillful when compared to the Distinct Teaching.
Among the three types of persons, the pratyekabuddha is the middling one.
Because the person of middling capacity understands the Dharma of the "common" (pāṭha) teaching, they are said to possess middling wisdom.

The Buddha and the bodhisattva of the distinct teaching both know the twelve links of dependent origination as they pertain to the realm beyond the world; compared to the Buddha, the successive bodhisattva is not yet superior, yet compared to those of the common and treasury teachings, this is a superior dharma. Therefore, it is appropriately designated by the name "superior wisdom."

In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contemplate the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination beyond the realms; from the very first thought-moment, they realize the Middle Way through phenomena.
Because this Dharma is most supreme and because it is appropriate to designate it by the name of the Buddha, it is called the contemplation of the highest-of-the-high wisdom.
The four teachings are used to explain the four contemplations, which is entirely consistent with the meaning, and so forth.

As for what is called "contemplation by means of inferior wisdom," it is the contemplation that feeling arises from contact; contact arises from the sense bases; the sense bases arise from name-and-form; name-and-form arises from consciousness; consciousness arises from volitional formations; and volitional formations arise from ignorance.
Ignorance, inversion, and unwholesome reflection lead to unwholesome conduct, which gives rise to consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth within the four realms of existence.
