If one reflects wholesomely, it leads to wholesome conduct, which gives rise to consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth among humans and devas.
Contemplate this ignorance: it is impermanent from moment to moment, never abiding from one instant to the next.
The good and evil that arise therein shift and change, rapidly decaying.
The name-and-form that are experienced undergo decline and replacement.
Afflictions, karma, and suffering serve as mutual causes and conditions for one another, never ceasing for even a moment.
There are two causes in the past resulting in five fruits in the present;
there are three causes in the present resulting in two fruits in the future.
The cycles of the three periods of time revolve like a chariot wheel.
Since the root of delusion is characterized by impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, ignorance is extinguished.
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, up to the cessation of old age and death.
If one does not kindle the fire, then there will be no smoke; this is called the severing of the son’s bonds.
Without seeds there is no fruit; when wisdom is extinguished and the body reduced to ashes, one departs from the twenty-five realms of existence—this is called the severance of the bond of fruit.
This is the inferior wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination and attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.
Regarding the wisdom of the middle [truth]: one contemplates that feeling arises from contact, and so on, up to volitional formations arising from ignorance.
Ignorance is merely a single moment of deluded mind; the mind has no form or substance, existing only as a name.
Searching for this word within, without, or in between, it cannot be found.
This word does not abide, nor does it not abide.
It is like a magical illusion, deceiving the eyes.
The essential nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) is fundamentally non-existent; it arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Because it has no real existence, it is conventionally designated as "ignorance.

It is produced by the mental activities of unwholesome reflection; because one does not realize that ignorance is like a magical illusion, one gives rise to wholesome and unwholesome reflections, which then result in wholesome and unwholesome formations (*saṃskāra*), and lead to the experience of wholesome and unwholesome name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
Now, because one realizes that ignorance is like an illusion, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are likewise like a magical transformation.
Consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth, which arise from illusion, are all like illusions.
Craving, grasping, becoming, and birth—the revolving cycle through the three periods of time—are illusory transformations and shifting changes; they possess no reality whatsoever.
A person of wisdom should not give rise to attachment or aversion toward this.
Since ignorance cannot be apprehended, ignorance does not arise; that which does not arise does not cease.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are likewise neither born nor extinguished.
Because they are not born, they are not new;
because they are not extinguished, they are not old.
That which is not old can be brought to an end because it has no prior existence;
that which is not new cannot be created because it has no novelty.
When there is no novelty, the bonds of the son are severed.
"Without cause" means that the bonds of the fruit are severed;
this is called the middle wisdom contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, by which one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
As for those with superior wisdom who contemplate, they observe that feeling arises from contact, and so on, up to formations arising from ignorance.
Ignorance is simply the single thought-moment of delusion.
Because the mind is deluded, afflictions branch out from it;
because of these afflictions, various karmas branch out.
Sufferings are produced by karma;
when one contemplates these afflictions, their specific types differ.
Because they differ, the karmas differ.
Because karma is not the same, suffering is not the same.
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are manifold, and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are each distinct.
The various three paths are immeasurable and boundless; they are distinguished without confusion.
One knows that because of these afflictions (*kleśa*), this karma arises, and this suffering is obtained; it does not concern that [other] karma or those [other] afflictions.
Thus, these three paths obscure and obstruct the three virtues (*guṇa*).
The skillful means for destroying hindrances are likewise immeasurable.
When ignorance is destroyed, prajñā is revealed;
when karma is destroyed, liberation is revealed.
When consciousness and name-and-form are destroyed, the Dharmakāya is revealed.
It is likewise with craving, grasping, becoming, and old age and death.
Having attained understanding for oneself, one is further able to transform others.
To know all phenomena in every respect and give rise to the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgajñatā*) in order to guide and benefit sentient beings—
this is called the superior wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination.

Regarding the observation by those of supreme wisdom: they observe that feeling arises from contact, and so on, up to volitional formations arising from ignorance. They know that the twelve links and the three paths are themselves the three virtues (*triguṇa*). How could one possibly sever or destroy the three virtues in order to seek the three virtues anew?
Thus, one would destroy the characteristics of all phenomena.
Afflictions are themselves prajñā; one should know that afflictions are not darkness.
Prajñā is itself afflictions; prajñā is not illumination.
Since afflictions are not inherently dark, why should they need to be severed?
Since Prajñā is not inherently luminous, what could it possibly destroy?
Darkness is fundamentally not darkness; thus, there is no need for light.
Just as Jīvaka takes poison and transforms it into medicine, how could one possibly discard this and take that?
If the path of karma is itself liberation, one should know that the path of karma is not bondage;
if liberation were identical to karma, then liberation would not be sovereignty.
Since karma is not a bondage, what is there to be abandoned?
Since liberation is not a state of mastery, what is there to be attained?
Is it as if a person with supernormal powers would ever avoid this place to go to that?
If the Path of Suffering is the Dharmakāya, one should know that suffering is not birth-and-death;
if the Dharmakāya is birth-and-death, the Dharmakāya is not bliss.
Since suffering is not birth-and-death, what is there to be grieved over?
The Dharma-body is not pleasure; what is there to rejoice in?
Like empty space, it is without gain or loss, neither elated nor dejected.

One who contemplates in this way sees that the three paths are not different from the three virtues, and the three virtues are not different from the three paths; furthermore, within the three paths, all Buddha-dharmas are fully present.
Why is this? The three paths are themselves the three virtues, and these three virtues are Great Nirvana, which is called the Secret Treasury; this constitutes the fruition of Buddhahood.
To deeply contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination is itself to sit at the site of enlightenment; this constitutes the cause of Buddhahood.
The causes of Buddhahood and the fruits of Buddhahood are both fully perfected; other cases may be understood by analogy.
This is called the supreme wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination and attains the Bodhi of a Buddha.
Based on this, one should judge what is coarse and what is subtle, and distinguish the coarse to reveal the subtle; since the underlying meaning is intelligible, I have not recorded it in detail.
Furthermore, when the four wisdoms illuminate the four objects, if those objects do not transform, then those wisdoms are coarse.
The four objects are transformed into sublime objects, and coarse wisdom becomes sublime wisdom; this still carries the sense of "relative" and "absolute," and so forth.
Second, regarding the clear understanding of the fourfold Four Noble Truths, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"There are two kinds of knowledge of the noble truths:"
There are middle wisdom and superior wisdom.
Middle wisdom refers to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
superior wisdom refers to all buddhas and bodhisattvas.
If one follows this text, combining the "substance" (體) and the "analysis" (析) is collectively termed "Middle.
Combining the "sharp" (利) and "dull" (鈍) faculties of the Mahāyāna is collectively termed "Superior.
Now, if we distinguish between sharp and dull faculties and conditions, as well as internal and external phenomena and principles, they open up into four categories:
The roots of the śrāvakas are dull; taking the phenomena of the Four Truths as their object, they possess the wisdom of the Four Truths regarding arising and ceasing.
The roots of the pratyekabuddhas are sharp; taking the principle of the Four Truths as their object, they possess the wisdom of the Four Truths regarding non-arising.
The wisdom of the bodhisattvas is shallow; taking inconceivable phenomena as their object, they possess the wisdom of the Four Truths regarding the immeasurable.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is profound; it takes the inconceivable principle as its object, which is precisely the wisdom of the four noble truths of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*).
This is a passage from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Furthermore, it says:
“Ordinary persons have suffering but no Truth; Śrāvakas have both suffering and the Truth of Suffering.
Because ordinary persons do not perceive the principle of suffering, it is said that they lack the Truth.
Because Śrāvakas are able to perceive impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, it is said that they possess the truths;
this refers precisely to the wisdom of the four truths of arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, it says:
"The Bodhisattva understands that suffering is without suffering, yet there is the True Reality (satya).
This means that by realizing that suffering is not [inherently] suffering, one says it is "without suffering";
because reality is found within phenomena themselves, one says there is "True Reality."
This is precisely the wisdom of the four truths of non-arising within the Mahāyāna gateway.
It is further said:
"To know that the aggregates (skandhas) are suffering, and to know that the sense bases (āyatanas) are gateways, is also called suffering."
"To know that the various elements (*dhātu*) are divisions, and to call this both 'nature' (*prakṛti*) and 'knowledge' (*jñāna*), is called middling wisdom.
According to what was previously stated, this refers to the Śrāvakas.

To discern the immeasurable characteristics of various sufferings, sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), yet say, "In that sutra, I did not speak of these at all"—this is called superior wisdom.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
This is not the domain of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; this point differs from the two preceding intentions.

Since it is called the wisdom of the superior intellect and is not the realm of the two vehicles, is this not precisely the contemplation by Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching upon the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha, which contains as many Buddha-dharmas as there are sands in the Ganges?
This constitutes the wisdom of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, it says:
"The Tathāgata is neither suffering, nor its origin, nor its cessation, nor the path; he is not a truth, yet this is the reality.
Space is neither suffering nor a truth, yet this is the reality."
"Not suffering" means it is not the false cycle of birth and death.
"Not a truth" means it is not the nirvana of the two vehicles.
"This is reality" refers to the true mark, the Middle Way, and the Buddha-nature.
It is further said:

"There is suffering, there is the cause of suffering, there is the cessation of suffering, and there is the remedy for suffering; the Tathāgata is neither suffering nor even the remedy. Therefore, he is the Real."
Since this elucidation of the meaning differs from the three preceding sections, is it not the wisdom of the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*)?
Following this pattern of one truth being treated as four, the same should apply to the remaining three.

That is to say: there is origination and the fruit of origination; there is the cessation of origination and the counteragent to origination; there is exhaustion and the cause of exhaustion; there is the obstacle to exhaustion and the characteristic of the obstacle to exhaustion; there is the counteragent and the fruit of the counteragent; and there is the obstacle to the counteragent and the characteristic of the obstacle to the counteragent.
The Tathāgata is not these sixteen types [of knowledge] consisting of four sets of four; rather, he speaks of them only in terms of the ultimate reality (*tattva*), and so forth.
Such wisdom contemplates the Four Truths.
Since the Truths have not yet been integrated, both the wisdom and the Truths remain coarse.
Only that which is neither suffering nor a truth, yet is real, is sublime.
If the truths are perfected, wisdom likewise becomes perfect; all of these are the Tathāgata’s sublime wisdom, which is neither suffering nor a truth, but is reality itself.
This refers to the two meanings of "relative" and "absolute," and so forth.
